# parquet - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/parquet/^58.3.0/

## Expand description

This crate contains the official Native Rust implementation of
[Apache Parquet](https://parquet.apache.org/), part of
the [Apache Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org/) project.
The crate provides a number of APIs to read and write Parquet files,
covering a range of use cases.

Please see the [parquet crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/parquet)
page for feature flags and tips to improve performance.

[§](https://docs.rs#format-overview)Format Overview

Parquet is a columnar format, which means that unlike row formats like [CSV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comma-separated_values), values are
iterated along columns instead of rows. Parquet is similar in spirit to [Arrow](https://docs.rs/arrow/latest/arrow/index.html), but
focuses on storage efficiency whereas Arrow prioritizes compute efficiency.

Parquet files are partitioned for scalability. Each file contains metadata, along with zero or more “row groups”, each row group containing one or more columns. The APIs in this crate reflect this structure.

Data in Parquet files is strongly typed and differentiates between logical
and physical types (see [ schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html)). In addition, Parquet files may contain
other metadata, such as statistics, which can be used to optimize reading
(see

[). For more details about the Parquet format itself, see the](https://docs.rs/file/metadata/index.html)

`file::metadata`[Parquet spec](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/master/README.md#file-format)

[§](https://docs.rs#apis)APIs

This crate exposes a number of APIs for different use-cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#metadata-and-schema)Metadata and Schema

The [ schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html) module provides APIs to work with Parquet schemas. The

[module provides APIs to work with Parquet metadata.](https://docs.rs/file/metadata/index.html)

`file::metadata`[§](https://docs.rs#reading-and-writing-arrow-arrow-feature)Reading and Writing Arrow (`arrow` feature)

The [ arrow](https://docs.rs/arrow/index.html) module supports reading and writing Parquet data to/from
Arrow

[es. Using Arrow is simple and performant, and allows workloads to leverage the wide range of data transforms provided by the](https://docs.rs/arrow/latest/arrow/array/struct.RecordBatch.html)

`RecordBatch`[arrow](https://docs.rs/arrow/latest/arrow/index.html)crate, and by the ecosystem of

[Arrow](https://docs.rs/arrow/latest/arrow/index.html)compatible systems.

Most users will use [ ArrowWriter](https://docs.rs/arrow/arrow_writer/struct.ArrowWriter.html) for writing and

[for reading from synchronous IO sources such as files or in-memory buffers.](https://docs.rs/arrow/arrow_reader/type.ParquetRecordBatchReaderBuilder.html)

`ParquetRecordBatchReaderBuilder`Lower level APIs include

- `ParquetPushDecoder`
- `ArrowColumnWriter`
- `RowFilter`

[§](https://docs.rs#experimental-content-defined-chunking)EXPERIMENTAL: Content-Defined Chunking

[ ArrowWriter](https://docs.rs/arrow/arrow_writer/struct.ArrowWriter.html) supports content-defined chunking (CDC), which creates data page
boundaries based on content rather than fixed sizes. CDC enables efficient
deduplication in content-addressable storage (CAS) systems: when the same data
appears in successive file versions, it will produce identical byte sequences that
CAS backends can deduplicate.

Enable CDC via [ WriterProperties](https://docs.rs/file/properties/struct.WriterProperties.html):

```
let props = WriterProperties::builder()
    .set_content_defined_chunking(Some(CdcOptions::default()))
    .build();
```
See [ CdcOptions](https://docs.rs/file/properties/struct.CdcOptions.html) for chunk size and normalization parameters.

[§](https://docs.rs#async-reading-and-writing-arrow-arrow-feature--async-feature)`async` Reading and Writing Arrow (`arrow` feature + `async` feature)

The [ async_reader](https://docs.rs/arrow/async_reader/index.html) and

[modules provide async APIs to read and write](https://docs.rs/arrow/async_writer/index.html)

`async_writer`[es asynchronously.](https://docs.rs/arrow/latest/arrow/array/struct.RecordBatch.html)

`RecordBatch`Most users will use [ AsyncArrowWriter](https://docs.rs/arrow/async_writer/struct.AsyncArrowWriter.html) for writing and

[for reading. When the](https://docs.rs/arrow/async_reader/type.ParquetRecordBatchStreamBuilder.html)

`ParquetRecordBatchStreamBuilder``object_store` feature is enabled, [provides efficient integration with object storage services such as S3 via the](https://docs.rs/arrow/async_reader/struct.ParquetObjectReader.html)

`ParquetObjectReader`[object_store](https://docs.rs/object_store/latest/object_store/)crate, automatically optimizing IO based on any predicates or projections provided.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant-logical-type-variant_experimental-feature)Variant Logical Type (`variant_experimental` feature)

The [ variant](https://docs.rs/variant/index.html) module supports reading and writing Parquet files
with the

[Variant Binary Encoding](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/master/VariantEncoding.md)logical type, which can represent semi-structured data such as JSON efficiently.

[§](https://docs.rs#readwrite-parquet-directly)Read/Write Parquet Directly

Workloads needing finer-grained control, or to avoid a dependence on arrow,
can use the APIs in [ file](https://docs.rs/file/index.html) directly. These APIs  are harder to use
as they directly use the underlying Parquet data model, and require knowledge
of the Parquet format, including the details of

[Dremel](https://research.google/pubs/pub36632/)record shredding and

[Logical Types](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/master/LogicalTypes.md).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [arrow](https://docs.rs/arrow/index.html)- `arrow`
- API for reading/writing Arrow `RecordBatch``Array`
- [basic](https://docs.rs/basic/index.html)

- APIs for reading parquet data.

- Automatically generated code from the Parquet thrift definition.

- Contains record-based API for reading Parquet files.
- [schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html)
- Parquet schema definitions and methods to print and parse schema.
- [thrift](https://docs.rs/thrift/index.html)
- Custom thrift definitions

# serde_json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_json/^1/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde-json)Serde JSON

JSON is a ubiquitous open-standard format that uses human-readable text to transmit data objects consisting of key-value pairs.

```
{
    "name": "John Doe",
    "age": 43,
    "address": {
        "street": "10 Downing Street",
        "city": "London"
    },
    "phones": [
        "+44 1234567",
        "+44 2345678"
    ]
}
```
There are three common ways that you might find yourself needing to work with JSON data in Rust.

- **As text data.**An unprocessed string of JSON data that you receive on an HTTP endpoint, read from a file, or prepare to send to a remote server.
- **As an untyped or loosely typed representation.**Maybe you want to check that some JSON data is valid before passing it on, but without knowing the structure of what it contains. Or you want to do very basic manipulations like insert a key in a particular spot.
- **As a strongly typed Rust data structure.**When you expect all or most of your data to conform to a particular structure and want to get real work done without JSON’s loosey-goosey nature tripping you up.

Serde JSON provides efficient, flexible, safe ways of converting data between each of these representations.

[§](https://docs.rs#operating-on-untyped-json-values)Operating on untyped JSON values

Any valid JSON data can be manipulated in the following recursive enum
representation. This data structure is [ serde_json::Value](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html).

```
enum Value {
    Null,
    Bool(bool),
    Number(Number),
    String(String),
    Array(Vec<Value>),
    Object(Map<String, Value>),
}
```
A string of JSON data can be parsed into a `serde_json::Value` by the
[ serde_json::from_str](https://docs.rs/fn.from_str.html) function. There is also

[for parsing from a byte slice](https://docs.rs/fn.from_slice.html)

`from_slice``&[u8]` and [for parsing from any](https://docs.rs/fn.from_reader.html)

`from_reader``io::Read` like a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde_json::{Result, Value};
fn untyped_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into serde_json::Value.
    let v: Value = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Access parts of the data by indexing with square brackets.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", v["name"], v["phones"][0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
The result of square bracket indexing like `v["name"]` is a borrow of the
data at that index, so the type is `&Value`. A JSON map can be indexed with
string keys, while a JSON array can be indexed with integer keys. If the
type of the data is not right for the type with which it is being indexed,
or if a map does not contain the key being indexed, or if the index into a
vector is out of bounds, the returned element is `Value::Null`.

When a `Value` is printed, it is printed as a JSON string. So in the code
above, the output looks like `Please call "John Doe" at the number "+44 1234567"`. The quotation marks appear because `v["name"]` is a `&Value`
containing a JSON string and its JSON representation is `"John Doe"`.
Printing as a plain string without quotation marks involves converting from
a JSON string to a Rust string with [ as_str()](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html#method.as_str) or avoiding the use of

`Value` as described in the following section.The `Value` representation is sufficient for very basic tasks but can be
tedious to work with for anything more significant. Error handling is
verbose to implement correctly, for example imagine trying to detect the
presence of unrecognized fields in the input data. The compiler is powerless
to help you when you make a mistake, for example imagine typoing `v["name"]`
as `v["nmae"]` in one of the dozens of places it is used in your code.

[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-json-as-strongly-typed-data-structures)Parsing JSON as strongly typed data structures

Serde provides a powerful way of mapping JSON data into Rust data structures largely automatically.

```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
fn typed_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into a Person object. This is exactly the
    // same function as the one that produced serde_json::Value above, but
    // now we are asking it for a Person as output.
    let p: Person = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Do things just like with any other Rust data structure.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", p.name, p.phones[0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
This is the same `serde_json::from_str` function as before, but this time we
assign the return value to a variable of type `Person` so Serde will
automatically interpret the input data as a `Person` and produce informative
error messages if the layout does not conform to what a `Person` is expected
to look like.

Any type that implements Serde’s `Deserialize` trait can be deserialized
this way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>`
and `HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Deserialize)]`.

Once we have `p` of type `Person`, our IDE and the Rust compiler can help us
use it correctly like they do for any other Rust code. The IDE can
autocomplete field names to prevent typos, which was impossible in the
`serde_json::Value` representation. And the Rust compiler can check that
when we write `p.phones[0]`, then `p.phones` is guaranteed to be a
`Vec<String>` so indexing into it makes sense and produces a `String`.

[§](https://docs.rs#constructing-json-values)Constructing JSON values

Serde JSON provides a [ json! macro](https://docs.rs/macro.json.html) to build

`serde_json::Value`
objects with very natural JSON syntax.```
use serde_json::json;
fn main() {
    // The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
    let john = json!({
        "name": "John Doe",
        "age": 43,
        "phones": [
            "+44 1234567",
            "+44 2345678"
        ]
    });
    println!("first phone number: {}", john["phones"][0]);
    // Convert to a string of JSON and print it out
    println!("{}", john.to_string());
}
```
The `Value::to_string()` function converts a `serde_json::Value` into a
`String` of JSON text.

One neat thing about the `json!` macro is that variables and expressions can
be interpolated directly into the JSON value as you are building it. Serde
will check at compile time that the value you are interpolating is able to
be represented as JSON.

```
let full_name = "John Doe";
let age_last_year = 42;
// The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
let john = json!({
    "name": full_name,
    "age": age_last_year + 1,
    "phones": [
        format!("+44 {}", random_phone())
    ]
});
```
This is amazingly convenient, but we have the problem we had before with
`Value`: the IDE and Rust compiler cannot help us if we get it wrong. Serde
JSON provides a better way of serializing strongly-typed data structures
into JSON text.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-json-by-serializing-data-structures)Creating JSON by serializing data structures

A data structure can be converted to a JSON string by
[ serde_json::to_string](https://docs.rs/fn.to_string.html). There is also

[which serializes to a](https://docs.rs/fn.to_vec.html)

`serde_json::to_vec``Vec<u8>` and
[which serializes to any](https://docs.rs/fn.to_writer.html)

`serde_json::to_writer``io::Write`
such as a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Address {
    street: String,
    city: String,
}
fn print_an_address() -> Result<()> {
    // Some data structure.
    let address = Address {
        street: "10 Downing Street".to_owned(),
        city: "London".to_owned(),
    };
    // Serialize it to a JSON string.
    let j = serde_json::to_string(&address)?;
    // Print, write to a file, or send to an HTTP server.
    println!("{}", j);
    Ok(())
}
```
Any type that implements Serde’s `Serialize` trait can be serialized this
way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>` and
`HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Serialize)]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

As long as there is a memory allocator, it is possible to use serde_json without the rest of the Rust standard library. Disable the default “std” feature and enable the “alloc” feature:

```
[dependencies]
serde_json = { version = "1.0", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
```
For JSON support in Serde without a memory allocator, please see the
[ serde-json-core](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/serde-json-core) crate.

# snafu - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/snafu/^0.9/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#snafu)SNAFU

SNAFU is a library to easily generate errors and add information to underlying errors, especially when the same underlying error type can occur in different contexts.

For detailed information, please see the [ Snafu](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html) macro and the

[user’s guide](https://docs.rs/guide/index.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- [Turnkey errors based on strings](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html)
- [Custom error types](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html)- Including a conversion path from turnkey errors

- [Backtraces](https://docs.rs/struct.Backtrace.html)
- Extension traits for
- [Error reporting](https://docs.rs#reporting)
- Suitable for libraries and applications
- `no_std`compatibility
- Generic types and lifetimes

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

If you want to report errors without hassle, start with the
[ Whatever](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html) type and the

[macro:](https://docs.rs/macro.whatever.html)

`whatever!````
use snafu::{prelude::*, Whatever};
fn is_valid_id(id: u16) -> Result<(), Whatever> {
    if id < 10 {
        whatever!("ID may not be less than 10, but it was {id}");
    }
    Ok(())
}
```
You can also use it to wrap any other error:

```
use snafu::{prelude::*, Whatever};
fn read_config_file(path: &str) -> Result<String, Whatever> {
    std::fs::read_to_string(path)
        .with_whatever_context(|_| format!("Could not read file {path}"))
}
```
[ Whatever](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html) allows for a short message and tracks a

[for every error:](https://docs.rs/struct.Backtrace.html)

`Backtrace````
use snafu::{prelude::*, ErrorCompat, Whatever};
if let Err(e) = returns_an_error() {
    eprintln!("An error occurred: {e}");
    if let Some(bt) = ErrorCompat::backtrace(&e) {
        eprintln!("{bt}");
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-error-types)Custom error types

Many projects will hit limitations of the `Whatever` type. When
that occurs, it’s time to create your own error type by deriving
[ Snafu](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html)!

[§](https://docs.rs#struct-style)Struct style

SNAFU will read your error struct definition and create a *context
selector* type (called `InvalidIdSnafu` in this example). These
context selectors are used with the [ ensure!](https://docs.rs/macro.ensure.html) macro to provide
ergonomic error creation:

```
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
#[snafu(display("ID may not be less than 10, but it was {id}"))]
struct InvalidIdError {
    id: u16,
}
fn is_valid_id(id: u16) -> Result<(), InvalidIdError> {
    ensure!(id >= 10, InvalidIdSnafu { id });
    Ok(())
}
```
If you add a `source` field to your error, you can then wrap an
underlying error using the [ context](https://docs.rs/trait.ResultExt.html#tymethod.context)
extension method:

```
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
#[snafu(display("Could not read file {path}"))]
struct ConfigFileError {
    source: std::io::Error,
    path: String,
}
fn read_config_file(path: &str) -> Result<String, ConfigFileError> {
    std::fs::read_to_string(path).context(ConfigFileSnafu { path })
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#enum-style)Enum style

While error structs are good for constrained cases, they don’t allow for reporting multiple possible kinds of errors at one time. Error enums solve that problem.

SNAFU will read your error enum definition and create a *context
selector* type for each variant (called `InvalidIdSnafu` in this
example). These context selectors are used with the [ ensure!](https://docs.rs/macro.ensure.html)
macro to provide ergonomic error creation:

```
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
enum Error {
    #[snafu(display("ID may not be less than 10, but it was {id}"))]
    InvalidId { id: u16 },
}
fn is_valid_id(id: u16) -> Result<(), Error> {
    ensure!(id >= 10, InvalidIdSnafu { id });
    Ok(())
}
```
If you add a `source` field to a variant, you can then wrap an
underlying error using the [ context](https://docs.rs/trait.ResultExt.html#tymethod.context)
extension method:

```
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
enum Error {
    #[snafu(display("Could not read file {path}"))]
    ConfigFile {
        source: std::io::Error,
        path: String,
    },
}
fn read_config_file(path: &str) -> Result<String, Error> {
    std::fs::read_to_string(path).context(ConfigFileSnafu { path })
}
```
You can combine the power of the [ whatever!](https://docs.rs/macro.whatever.html) macro with an
enum error type. This is great if you started out with

[and are moving to a custom error type:](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html)

`Whatever````
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
enum Error {
    #[snafu(display("ID may not be less than 10, but it was {id}"))]
    InvalidId { id: u16 },
    #[snafu(whatever, display("{message}"))]
    Whatever {
        message: String,
        #[snafu(source(from(Box<dyn std::error::Error>, Some)))]
        source: Option<Box<dyn std::error::Error>>,
    },
}
fn is_valid_id(id: u16) -> Result<(), Error> {
    ensure!(id >= 10, InvalidIdSnafu { id });
    whatever!("Just kidding... this function always fails!");
    Ok(())
}
```
You may wish to make the type `Send` and/or `Sync`, allowing
your error type to be used in multithreaded programs, by changing
`dyn std::error::Error` to `dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync`.

[§](https://docs.rs#reporting)Reporting

Printing an error via [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html)
will only show the top-level error message without the underlying sources.
For an extended error report,
SNAFU offers a user-friendly error output mechanism.
It prints the main error and all underlying errors in the chain,
from the most recent to the oldest,
plus the

[backtrace](https://docs.rs/struct.Backtrace.html)if applicable. This is done by using the

[procedural macro or the](https://docs.rs/attr.report.html)

`report`[type directly.](https://docs.rs/struct.Report.html)

`Report````
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
#[snafu(display("Could not load configuration file {path}"))]
struct ConfigFileError {
    source: std::io::Error,
    path: String,
}
fn read_config_file(path: &str) -> Result<String, ConfigFileError> {
    std::fs::read_to_string(path).context(ConfigFileSnafu { path })
}
#[snafu::report]
fn main() -> Result<(), ConfigFileError> {
    read_config_file("bad-config.ini")?;
    Ok(())
}
```
This will print:

```
Error: Could not load configuration file bad-config.ini
Caused by this error:
1: No such file or directory (os error 2)
```
Which shows the underlying errors, unlike [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html):

`Error: Could not load configuration file bad-config.ini`… and is also more readable than the [ Debug](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html) output:

`Error: ConfigFileError { source: Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, message: "No such file or directory" }, path: "bad-config.ini" }`[§](https://docs.rs#next-steps)Next steps

Read the documentation for the [ Snafu](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html) macro to see all of the
capabilities, then read the

[user’s guide](https://docs.rs/guide/index.html)for deeper understanding.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [futures](https://docs.rs/futures/index.html)- `futures`
- Additions to the `TryFuture``TryStream`

- SNAFU user’s guide

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [ensure](https://docs.rs/macro.ensure.html)
- Ensure a condition is true. If it is not, return from the function with an error.
- [ensure_](https://docs.rs/macro.ensure_whatever.html)- whatever - `alloc`
- Ensure a condition is true. If it is not, return a stringly-typed error message.
- [location](https://docs.rs/macro.location.html)
- Constructs a `Location`
- [whatever](https://docs.rs/macro.whatever.html)- `alloc`
- Instantiate and return a stringly-typed error message.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Backtrace](https://docs.rs/struct.Backtrace.html)
- A captured OS thread stack backtrace.
- [Chain](https://docs.rs/struct.ChainCompat.html)- Compat
- An iterator over an Error and its sources.
- [Cleaned](https://docs.rs/struct.CleanedErrorText.html)- Error - Text - `alloc`
- An iterator over an Error and its sources that removes duplicated text from the error display strings.
- [None](https://docs.rs/struct.NoneError.html)- Error
- A temporary error type used when converting an `Option``Result`
- [Report](https://docs.rs/struct.Report.html)
- Opinionated solution to format an error in a user-friendly
way. Useful as the return type from `main`and test functions.
- [Whatever](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html)- `alloc`
- A basic error type that you can use as a first step to better error handling.
- [Whatever](https://docs.rs/struct.WhateverLocal.html)- Local - `alloc`
- A basic error type that you can use as a first step to better error handling when the error does not need to cross a thread boundary.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [AsBacktrace](https://docs.rs/trait.AsBacktrace.html)
- View a backtrace-like value as an optional backtrace.
- [AsError](https://docs.rs/trait.AsErrorSource.html)- Source
- Converts the receiver into an `Error``Error::source`
- [Error](https://docs.rs/trait.ErrorCompat.html)- Compat
- Backports changes to the `Error`
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromString.html)- String - `alloc`
- Takes a string message and builds the corresponding error.
- [Generate](https://docs.rs/trait.GenerateImplicitData.html)- Implicit - Data
- Construct data to be included as part of an error. The data must require no arguments to be created.
- [Into](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoError.html)- Error
- Combines an underlying error with additional information about the error.
- [Option](https://docs.rs/trait.OptionExt.html)- Ext
- Additions to `Option`
- [Result](https://docs.rs/trait.ResultExt.html)- Ext
- Additions to `Result`

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Location](https://docs.rs/type.Location.html)
- The source code location where the error was reported.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [report](https://docs.rs/attr.report.html)
- Adapts a function to provide user-friendly error output for `main`functions and tests.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Snafu](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html)
- The `Snafu`macro is the entrypoint to defining your own error types. It is designed to require little configuration for the recommended and typical usecases while still offering flexibility for unique situations.
